1247.title: Vasishtha asks, what did I do?
1247.hook: a friend goes quiet. In a Rig Veda hymn, the seer Vasishtha goes to Varuna and asks: what did I do? Why Hindus still ask forgiveness at the end of puja
1247.carry: a wrong breaks rita; honest asking mends it
1247.tomorrow: a nurse walks out at dawn. what did the poets sing to it?
1247.howItsDone: Hymns to Varuna are read in Hindu tradition as prayers for release from wrongdoing, and many families still close a puja with a prayer asking God's forgiveness for any mistakes made, known or unknown.

segments.voice: The messages used to come every day. Jokes, photos, long voice notes. Now a friend answers in one word, or not at all. Something happened, but what? You scroll back looking for the moment it changed. A mutual friend shrugs: seems like they're upset with you. So there's one honest move left, and it's the hardest: go to the friend and ask, what did I do? A Rig Veda poet makes exactly that move, and the one he asks is a god.
screen: `THE MESSAGES GO QUIET.` → `SEEMS LIKE THEY'RE UPSET.` → `WHAT DID I DO?`

segments.voice: The god is Varuna. In the hymns, Varuna keeps rita, the right order of things, and he sees what people do. The poet is Vasishtha, a seer tradition remembers as the voice of these hymns. In paraphrase, Vasishtha says: I ask about this wrong, Varuna, wanting to understand. I go to the wise to ask, and the sages all tell me the same thing: Varuna is angry with you. So he turns to Varuna himself. What was my great offense, he asks, that you would strike the friend who sings your praise? Tell me, and I'll come to you quickly, bowing, free of it. He asks to be released from the wrongs of his fathers, and from the ones he did himself. Then this. It wasn't my own will, Varuna. It was drink, anger, the dice, thoughtlessness. The older one leads the younger astray. Even sleep doesn't keep wrongdoing away. Some readers hear an excuse in that. Others hear a man naming his weak spots out loud. Either way, he doesn't hide them. Here's the teaching under it. For the Vedic poets, a wrong isn't only a broken rule. It knocks rita, the right order that holds the world together, out of true, and it strains a bond with God, whom Vasishtha calls his friend. The way back is to own the wrong out loud and ask to be set right. That thread never left Hinduism. Many families still close a puja by asking God's forgiveness for any mistake, known or unknown.

segments.voice: Do what many families do at the end of a puja: ask forgiveness for what went wrong, known or unknown. Let one strained bond come to mind and, instead of arguing your side, ask quietly: what part of this is mine? Name it plainly, as Vasishtha named drink and anger and dice. If you pray, bring it to God and ask to be set right; if not, just hold it honestly.

1248.hook: a night-shift nurse walks out into a sky going pink. The Rig Veda sings to that light, Ushas, the dawn, and it's why Hindus greet the morning sun

segments.voice: The hospital doors slide open and a nurse steps out after a long night shift. Her feet hurt. Her head is full of beeping. Then she looks up. The sky over the parking lot is going from gray to rose to gold, and for a second she forgets everything else. The birds have started. A bus hisses at the corner. Plenty of mornings like this go by unseen. The Rig Veda's poets turned to that light, gave it a name, and sang to it. Today, Ushas, the dawn.
screen: `OUT OF THE NIGHT SHIFT.` → `GRAY, ROSE, GOLD.` → `THE POETS SANG TO IT.`

segments.voice: In the Rig Veda, Ushas is a goddess, pictured as a young woman in bright clothes, driving away the dark. One hymn to her begins, in paraphrase: this light has come, the fairest of lights. Her bright sign is born. Then the poet notices time. The night has made room for the dawn, like a sister giving way to her sister. And then this line. Gone are the mortals who watched the earlier dawns. Now she is seen by us. And coming are those who will see her in mornings still ahead. Three groups of people under one light: those before us, us, and those after. Every sunrise, on this reading, joins them. Later the hymn wakes everyone up. Rise, it says. The breath of life has come back to us. The dark has gone away. Light is coming near. She has opened a path for the sun to travel. And she is ancient and young at once, the hymn says, coming again and again. Here's why that matters in a Hindu home. Dawn is a sandhya, one of the day's holy junctions, with noon and dusk. For many Hindus it's a time to bathe, pray, and pour water toward the rising sun. The poets taught that morning light isn't just weather. It's sacred, and it's shared: whoever greets it stands where their grandparents stood, and where their grandchildren will.

segments.voice: Turn toward the east or a window if you can, or call a dawn you remember to mind. Do what many Hindus do each morning: if you have a cup of water, lift it toward the light and pour a little slowly into a plant; if not, just lift your open hands. Hold three people in that light: someone before you who saw this sky, someone with you now, someone who will see it after you. If you pray, greet the morning in your own words.

segments.voice: He promised. No more, not this time. He walks past the casino floor toward the exit, proud of himself. Then, from behind a row of machines, comes the bright little jingle of someone winning. His feet slow. The promise was real, and so is the pull, and the pull is winning. One Rig Veda hymn is spoken by a gambler, in his own voice, and it doesn't hold back.
screen: `HE PROMISED. HE MEANT IT.` → `THEN THE SOUND OF WINNING.` → `A GAMBLER'S HYMN.`

segments.voice: He starts with the dice themselves. They thrill me, he says, in paraphrase, like a deep drink of soma. Then he tells what they cost. My wife never quarreled with me, never got angry. She was kind to me and to my friends. And for the sake of one losing throw, I drove away a devoted wife. Now his mother-in-law hates him, his wife pushes him away, and his own family says: we don't know him, take him away. Then the line the hymn turns on. When I decide I won't play, he says, I fall behind as my friends go off. But when the brown dice are thrown and their sound reaches me, off I go to the meeting place like a lover to a lover. His resolve doesn't fail from lack of knowing better. It fails at the sound. Then a voice cuts through. Don't play with dice. Farm your field. Be glad of what you have, and value it. There are your cattle, there is your wife. So says Savitar, the god who rouses, linked with the sun. That's a real Hindu teaching, and an old one. Life has room for wealth and pleasure, but inside dharma: the duty you owe the people who count on you. The householder's path is honest work, a home kept, a family cared for, and the dice break all three. Hindus know where that road goes. The Mahabharata turns on a dice game, where Yudhishthira stakes his kingdom, his brothers, himself, and Draupadi.

segments.voice: Think of one pull that gets past your good intentions, a phone, a bet, an old argument, and without scolding yourself, notice its trigger. segments.voice: Run the day backward, like a video on rewind. Dinner un-cooks. The drive home un-drives. Morning coffee pours itself back into the pot. Keep going. The house comes apart into lumber, the lumber into trees, the trees into seeds. Past the first people, the first mountains, the first stars. At some point the rewind has nothing left to rewind. What's there? Or is there even a there? One Rig Veda hymn stops at that last frame and stares at it. You glimpsed it on day one thousand fifty-seven. Today, the Nasadiya Sukta's first verse.
screen: `RUN THE DAY BACKWARD.` → `PAST THE FIRST STARS.` → `NOTHING LEFT TO REWIND.`

segments.voice: The hymn takes its name from its first words, na asat: not non-being. In paraphrase it opens: then there was not non-being, and there was not being. There was no air, and no sky beyond it. It doesn't say, in the beginning there was nothing. It says even nothing wasn't there yet. The usual pair of opposites, is and isn't, hasn't started. And then, instead of an answer, the poet asks questions. What covered it? Where? In whose keeping? Was there water, deep beyond measure? That's the whole first verse: a hymn about creation that begins by refusing to describe it, and asks instead. Some readers hear wonder in that. Some hear a careful thinker, unwilling to claim more than anyone could know. Some Hindu teachers hear a picture of Brahman before names and forms. The hymn doesn't say which. It simply puts the questions into the sacred collection, to be chanted. They weren't left at the edge of scripture as doubts. They were kept inside it. That's a teaching in itself. Hinduism has no single creation story you must sign on to: the Rig Veda alone holds several, and the Puranas tell more. And honest asking is treated as holy. Many Upanishads are built as conversations, a student asking, a teacher answering. In this tradition the question isn't the enemy of faith. It's chanted with the rest.

segments.voice: The first verse cleared away being and non-being, air and sky. The second keeps clearing. In paraphrase: there was no death then, and no deathlessness. No sign to tell night from day. Death and its opposite, the undying: gone. Night and day, the rhythm a life runs on: gone, or not yet. And then, for the first time in the hymn, something is. That One breathed, the verse says, without wind, by its own power. Apart from it, there was nothing else at all. Not a god with a name. Not Agni, not Indra, not Varuna. Just That One, tad ekam. And not doing anything grand. It breathes. Breath is life, but here there's no air, so the breath is windless, moved by nothing outside itself. Readers take That One in different ways. Vedanta teachers in Shankara's line hear Brahman, prior to every name. Other Hindu readers hear the Lord before the work of creation. Some hear a poet pushing language as far as it goes and finding only a breath. The verse doesn't decide for them. But here's what it plants. A few days ago you met the verse that says what is one, the wise speak of in many ways. This hymn reaches further back, before Agni, Indra or Varuna had names, to That One. It's a seed of a teaching that runs all through Hinduism: many gods, many names, and one reality underneath, which the Upanishads will call Brahman.

segments.voice: Stop managing the breath: don't deepen it or slow it, just watch it go on its own, rising and falling with nothing outside pushing it, and rest in the stillness around it. When the mind starts to explain the breath, let the explanation go and come back to the plain fact of it; if you pray, you can rest in that breath as a gift.

1252.title: Born of tapas
1252.hook: the power goes out on a night with no moon. In the creation hymn's dark, the One is born of tapas, heat: why Hindus fast and keep vows
1252.carry: tapas: the holy heat of discipline
1252.tomorrow: which comes first, a thought or a want?
1252.howItsDone: Many Hindus keep vratas, vows, and fasts such as Ekadashi, understood as tapas: a discipline offered to God. The Nasadiya Sukta itself is kept in traditional recitation, learned by memory from a teacher.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-FIFTY-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, That One: one reality, before every name. Before night or day, That One breathed without wind.
screen: `THAT ONE BREATHED WITHOUT WIND.`

segments.voice: The power goes out on a night with no moon. You shut your eyes, then open them, and can't tell the difference. The dark behind your eyelids and the dark of the room have become one dark. Your hand is somewhere in front of your face, but you couldn't prove it. Nothing has an edge. The Nasadiya Sukta's third verse begins in that kind of dark, and pushes it further than any power cut could.
screen: `THE POWER GOES OUT.` → `EYES OPEN, EYES SHUT: THE SAME.` → `NOTHING HAS AN EDGE.`

segments.voice: In Sanskrit the verse opens tama asit tamasa gulham agre. Darkness there was, hidden by darkness, in the beginning. Not darkness covering something: darkness covering darkness. Nothing to see, and nothing to see it with. In paraphrase it goes on: all this was water, with no mark on it, nothing told apart from anything else. That's the hymn's picture of the start: not an empty space with sharp edges, but a sameness so complete that nothing could stand out. Then the turn. What was coming into being lay covered by emptiness, and that One was born by the power of tapas. Tapas is a word for heat. And here's the part to tell a friend tonight: the same word names the heat a person builds through vows, fasting and long prayer. Notice what the verse leaves out. It doesn't say who made the heat, or name a god striking a spark. First, sameness, dark on dark. Then warmth. Then one thing that could be told apart. Later texts take the thread further. The Taittiriya Upanishad says the One wished to become many, performed tapas, and having done it, made all this. So when a grandmother fasts on Ekadashi, or a family keeps a vow through a festival, the tradition doesn't see mere going without. It sees tapas: the same warm power the world was born from, building in a person, and offered to God.
screen: `DARKNESS HIDDEN BY DARKNESS.` · `WATER WITH NO MARK ON IT.` · `THE ONE, BORN BY THE POWER OF TAPAS.` · `FASTS AND VOWS: TAPAS TODAY.` · then, large: `TAPAS: THE HOLY HEAT OF DISCIPLINE.`

segments.voice: Choose one small vow for today, the way families keep a vrata: one meal kept simple, no phone for the first hour, or one kind thing done without being thanked. Then close your eyes or lower your gaze, let the dark be plain, and find one warm place, the hands resting together or the middle of the chest. Rest there, holding the vow, coming back whenever a thought pulls you off. If you pray, offer the vow to God; if not, keep it for someone you love.

1253.title: Desire, the first seed
1253.hook: which comes first in a morning, a thought or a want? The creation hymn says desire, and Hindu teaching says desire isn't the enemy
1253.carry: kama: desire is a seed, guided by dharma
1253.tomorrow: a cord stretched across the dark. whose is it?
1253.howItsDone: Hindu teachers and commentators read the Nasadiya Sukta's lines on desire and the searching poets in several ways, and its verses are kept in traditional Vedic recitation learned from a teacher.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-FIFTY-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the One was born by tapas: the holy heat of discipline, the reason Hindus fast and keep vows.
screen: `DARKNESS, THEN HEAT, THEN ONE.`

segments.voice: Which comes first in a morning, a thought or a want? Watch the first minute after an alarm. Before a plan forms, there's often a lean. Toward the warm blanket. Toward coffee. Toward the phone on the nightstand. Only after the lean does the mind start talking, building reasons, making a list. The Nasadiya Sukta asks that question on the largest scale there is. The One has just been born out of the dark. What happens next? The fourth verse answers, and its answer is not a thought.
screen: `A THOUGHT OR A WANT?` → `FIRST, A LEAN.` → `THEN THE MIND STARTS TALKING.`

segments.voice: The verse opens with kama. Desire came upon it in the beginning, it says, desire that was the first seed of mind. Kama is the ordinary Sanskrit word for desire, wanting, love. And here it stands at the very start, before mind. Not desire as a problem to be fixed: desire as a seed. First the wanting, then the mind that grows out of it. Then the verse turns from the cosmos to people. The poets, the kavis, searched in their hearts with wisdom, and found the bond of what is in what is not. The word for bond is bandhu. It also means kin, the people you're tied to. So the poets found that being has a kinship with non-being, a family tie running back into the dark. Notice where they looked: not at the sky, but in the heart. So the hymn doesn't make desire the enemy, and neither does Hindu teaching as a whole. Kama is one of the four aims of a human life, beside dharma, artha and moksha: right living, honest wealth, and freedom. What matters is the order. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says, among beings, I am desire that isn't against dharma. Desire steered by dharma is holy. Desire that runs over dharma is the gambler at the dice. The week began with Vasishtha owning his wrong, and it ends here: the wanting comes first, and dharma steers it.
screen: `KAMA: DESIRE, THE FIRST SEED OF MIND.` · `THE POETS SEARCHED IN THEIR HEARTS.` · `FOUR AIMS: DHARMA, ARTHA, KAMA, MOKSHA.` · `GITA: DESIRE NOT AGAINST DHARMA.` · then, large: `DESIRE, STEERED BY DHARMA.`

segments.voice: Let the breath run on its own and wait for the next thought; when it comes, don't follow it, but look just underneath for the want that came first: to be comfortable, to be finished, to be loved. Don't judge it or feed it. Ask the Gita's question of it: does this want go with dharma, or against it? Then come back to the breath. If you pray, you can offer each want as you find it.
